When you pay off your credit card, the money goes to the bank. The global economy doesn’t change.
But the federal government isn’t a bank. It’s the source of the money.
Every dollar the government spends and doesn’t tax back becomes a dollar held
by somebody else. That can be a household, a business, a pension fund, or a foreign

This all means the $40-ish trillion number that gets waved around on cable news is
not a bill anyone is going to be handed. It’s a ledger of what everybody else owns.

Every single dollar of debt they erase is a dollar of someone’s savings wiped out. The
country doesn’t get richer. But the people get poorer. Money doesn’t go as far, they are left
with less cash and need to borrow to stay afloat. Paying off the national debt isn’t like paying off
a credit card. It’s the government draining your savings accounts and calling it responsibility.
And the political narrative about who we owe that money to is completely backwards.
The phrase ‘National Debt’ makes you think that the U.S. owes money
to foreign powers. But that’s not the case. Of the roughly $40 trillion in total federal debt,
about $7.6 trillion is intragovernmental. It’s owed to itself. The Treasury owes
that money to federal trust funds, like Social Security and Medicare. Those trust funds don’t
keep their cash in a vault. They hold Treasury securities. Wipe out the national debt and you
wipe out the programs keeping the elderly alive. The Federal Reserve holds around $4.4 trillion in
Treasury securities. The rest belongs to pension funds, insurance companies, commercial banks,
state governments, and ordinary savers. Foreign holdings come to only around $9.35 trillion,
about a quarter of the total. China, the country politicians constantly scream r about,
holds roughly $651 billion and has been dumping American debt for over a decade..
So when a politician promises to pay it all back, they’re not being
entirely honest. What they really mean is emptying the Social Security trust fund,
retiring the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet, and eviscerating every pension fund in America.
And that’s just the accounting side. The reality is much worse. Because in 1835,
Treasury bonds were an investment. In 2026, they’re infrastructure.
Every single day, the world’s banks, hedge funds, money market funds, and pension funds need to move
enormous amounts of cash between each other. And they do it without taking a risk on the others’
credit. They use the shadow banking system, or the repo market. One bank hands over a security,
and the other hands over cash. The next morning, they swap back with a little interest.
Nobody is lending on trust. They’re lending against the security.
No one actually knew how big this market was until recently, because a huge chunk of it
operates in the dark, off any public exchange. When the Office of Financial Research, or OFR,
got their hands on the data, they discovered roughly $12.6 trillion in daily exposures.
$12.6 trillion. Every single day.
The data also revealed that nearly 70% of borrowed money is backed by the U.S.
Treasury. And in the clearing house, the part of the industry that can’t fall,
that figure ramped up to 88.9%. There’s a reason for this.
A Treasury bond is one of the only assets on Earth that’s simultaneously big enough, liquid enough
and safe enough to keep everything moving. When there’s a shortage, the financial world panics.
Not even gold can save the day. If you took the entire above-ground
stock of gold on Earth it barely covers two days of the overnight market.
But there’s a second reason that makes Treasuries completely irreplaceable.
One that almost nobody outside the industry knows about.
A Treasury security can get reused multiple times. At the same time. A hedge fund posts a bond to a
dealer to borrow cash. That dealer takes the same bond and hands it to a bank to borrow cash for
themselves. The bank does it too. One piece of paper secures a chain of loans stretching
across continents in a single afternoon. Economists call it collateral re-use.
It’s actually a phantom system. It works almost like a traditional
bank run. Your bank lends most of its deposits out to you and a bunch of strangers. You all
think you have a claim on the same money. The system works fine until everyone asks for their
money at once. This creates a bank run. Follow that logic to bonds, and the danger
becomes catastrophic. If a chain of transactions is built on a bond being used over and over again,
removing that security snaps the entire chain everywhere, instantly.
We’ve seen this play out on a small scale. In September 2019, two routine events happened
on the same day: quarterly corporate tax payments came due, and $54 billion of long-term Treasury
debt settled. Both of those pulled cash out of the banking system. According to the Federal
Reserve’s own post-mortem, reserves in the banking system dropped by about $120 billion
over 2 business days. The system seized.
The Secured Overnight Financing Rate (or SOFR), the benchmark rate for overnight
borrowing against Treasury collateral, more than doubled. It went from 2.43% on September 16th to
over 5% on September 17. The cost of borrowing money broke through the Fed’s own target range.
But it didn’t have to happen. There was plenty of money
sitting on the sidelines. Lenders could have stepped in
and made a fortune in a single morning, but they couldn’t. The money market funds, pension funds,
and banks all stayed put, and borrowers, unable to go anywhere else, paid whatever was demanded.
The Federal Reserve Bank of New York had to step in the next morning directly,
offering up to $75 billion in overnight repo and injecting $53 billion in reserves. It kept
doing it every morning for the rest of the week. Every operation was fully subscribed. By October,
it was buying $60 billion of Treasury bills a month to keep the system moving.
How did this happen? The government had issued a
record number of bonds, but the banking system ran out of cash needed to trade them. There
wasn’t enough money to go around the collateral. Now imagine removing the collateral permanently.
We don’t need to guess what happens next. The evidence is already there. Over the last
2 centuries, the U.S. had made 6 major attempts at reducing the federal debt.
Each time was a massacre. Every significant reduction
of the national debt in American history was followed by a depression. For two centuries,
the pattern held without an outlier. Mainstream economists will say this is
correlation rather than causation. Each of those crises had separate causes, such as cotton prices,
railroad speculation, silver, crop failures, or an absent central bank. But when a government
runs a surplus to pay down its debt, it takes cash from the everyday economy. That means more
borrowing from businesses and everyday people. And when the private sector begins to drown in debt,
the entire system becomes fragile. Then it shatters.
One nation actually achieved what American politicians keep promising.
And it kicked off a new dark age for the country. In the 1970s, Romania borrowed heavily from
Western banks to industrialize. By 1982, its external debt had peaked at around $13 billion.
Then interest rates spiked, the global economy slowed, and Romania couldn’t pay.
Other developing countries in exactly that position negotiated, but dictator Nicolae
Ceaușescu decided Romania would pay every cent. In practice, everything a Romanian consumed had to be
converted into a foreign-currency export. Imports were crushed. Domestic energy was redirected into
factories producing goods for sale abroad. By 1983, the standard of living had fallen
by between 19 and 40%. Then it got specific.
Ceaușescu launched what was called a “Rational Eating Program” because Romanians were eating
too much. It set out to cut the national calorie intake to between 2,800 and 3,000
calories a day. By December 1983, a new plan for the following year set the allowances even lower.
Rationing began in 1981 for bread, milk, cooking oil, sugar and meat. From 1982,
people in the cities were told that bread could only be bought on a non-transferable ration card.
In 1984, the standards entitled a Romanian citizen to 86 pounds (39 kilograms) of meat for the year.
That’s about a quarter-pound burger a day… if you were lucky enough to find any.
The regime also began building enormous domed food distribution halls across
Bucharest as showpieces of socialist plenty. Romanians called them hunger circuses.
Hot water was available one day a week in most apartments. Private car owners could
buy 30 liters (or about eight gallons) of petrol a month. Street lighting was cut to almost nothing
and often switched off entirely. In 1985, regional radio stations were shut down, and television was
reduced to a single channel broadcasting 2 to 3 hours a day, to save electricity.
But by March 1989, virtually all of Romania’s external debt had been repaid. The CIA World
Factbook listed Romania’s external debt in mid-1989 as “none.” A decree was
passed making it illegal for Romanian entities to borrow abroad ever again.
The ration cards were withdrawn on Christmas Eve 1989. Mainly because 2 days earlier, Ceaușescu
had fled the roof of the Central Committee building in a helicopter. On Christmas Day,
he was caught, tried in front of a camera for 55 minutes, stood up against a wall, and shot. Today,
Romania’s government debt is projected to be about 62% of its total GDP in 2026.
So why does the ‘no debt’ promise keep coming back?
Because it’s the ambitious and often less-understood center of American
politics. It’s been that way for decades. In January 2000, former President Bill
Clinton delivered the State of the Union with 7 years of falling deficits behind him and a
projected surplus running to the horizon. In his words, if the country stayed on that path,
it could pay down the debt entirely in 13 years. The U.S. would be debt-free for the first time
since Andrew Jackson was president in 1835. The 2001 budget would retire the $3.6 trillion
held by the public by 2013, 2 years ahead of the original schedule. In February,
Clinton stood in front of a chart captioned “America: Debt Free by 2013” and drew the
curve down to zero with a marker. In March 2016, Donald Trump told the
Washington Post the country has to get rid of its $19 trillion in debt. When asked how long
that would take, he said 8 years. A decade later, the gross debt
had doubled instead, past $40 trillion. But for one brief window around the turn
of the millennium, Clinton’s promise looked like it might genuinely happen, and people panicked.
In March 2001, Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan stood in front of the
House Budget Committee and said something that terrified them. The U.S. was on track
to clear its debt by the end of the decade. He warned that if the government kept running
surpluses when it was debt free, the state would have to pump cash into the private stock
market. The government would end up owning American industry completely by accident.
Economist Alice Rivlin called it the peril of zero debt.
Behind the scenes, officials at the Fed and the Treasury scrambled to find the answers
to questions no one had asked before. How do you run a country that has no
government bonds? What does the central bank buy? What do the banks post as collateral?
Emergency talks were held as the crisis loomed in the distance. The Fed chairman
argued for a tax cut, desperately trying to stop the government paying off the debt.
No one had an answer. No one wanted to find out.
But there is one more way to reach a zero balance. Defaulting on the debt.
The United States can’t run out of dollars. It holds the monopoly on creating the currency. Every
single piece of Treasury debt is denominated in dollars. There’s no scenario in which the
government is unable to pay its bills. The only way America defaults is if it chooses to or if
it makes it illegal for itself to pay. This is exactly what the debt ceiling
does. Congress sets a statutory cap on borrowing. Once it’s hit, the Treasury
is legally barred from issuing new securities while remaining perfectly capable of paying.
In this scenario, the choices get ugly fast. Federal Reserve transcripts from August 2011
confirmed there was a contingency plan to pay bondholders first and delay everything
else. That included federal salaries, contractor invoices, and benefit payments.
So a default doesn’t destroy Treasuries. It just destroys the certainty surrounding it.
The moment a Treasury security can miss a payment, every clearing house and repo
desk on Earth has to change its calculations and post more collateral for the same cash.
You can pay the debt off, and the collateral vanishes. Or you can default on it and the
collateral becomes worthless. Both roads end at a financial system with no universally accepted
way to lend money overnight. That doesn’t mean the U.S.
national debt is harmless. When the government owes $40 trillion,
interest payments cannibalize everything else. But the real problem isn’t the size of the debt,
it’s the architecture. It’s about how much of it is short-term,
who’s willing to buy it over and what happens to the global cost of living if anyone hesitates.
That’s an argument you won’t hear on television. “Reduce the deficit” and “eliminate the debt” are
different propositions. Political language folds them into one talking point because
it’s easier to sell to the public. The world needs a financial asset that
is enormous, liquid, and certain. Only one institution on Earth can manufacture it. The
manufacturing process is called deficit spending, and the finished product is called the national
debt. That’s the unavoidable obligation the United States took on the moment the dollar became the
currency the rest of the planet works in. If you destroy it, the whole thing comes
crashing down. And you’re left standing at a checkout. Holding a card that doesn’t work…
In a country that just did exactly what it promised.
